PROCEEDINGS
I just want to verify that you were born August 11th, 1908, right?
Right.
That's the right date.
Yeah.
And I just want you to tell me about how you started out. I know your brother Bill played several instruments and your parents also played, right? Tell me about it. Was it an older brother?

Yes, I was the youngest of three brothers in my family. I had one sister. She was -- she's the youngest, but I was the youngest brother, and we all played, you know, as children. We took music, you know, not intending to be professional musicians, but it was just part of our education. My father studied violin but never played anyplace. He just studied and studied and played at home. And my mother, who played piano and sang in the church choir, and that's how it all began. My brother and I, we started when we were six years old, with the violin. We took violin lessons. We started out and it's a funny thing, I took to it. When I first got a violin in my hands it was just like it was something I really liked. You know, with no thought of being a professional musician at all. I just liked it and I loved it, because, you know, well, I just loved it. It did a lot of things for me.

And before that I remember as far back as, I think -- as I always say, I remember when I was three years old, three and a half years old, four years old. We lived in Long Island, and you know, we used to have a big, large dining room. We had a fireplace and everything, you know. My father would come home in the evening, and after dinner my mother would play the piano and he'd play the violin and there's one incident that my mother always talked about. They were playing something on the piano. I don't know what it was. They used to play things like, "Poet and Peasant", and that sort of thing, and whatever they were playing, it just got to me, you know, and I just ran and jumped up on her lap and, you know, just like I was -- you know, like the music just --
Possessed you.

Possessed, I suppose, yeah. It just moved me like that, you know. And all through my life, you know, right now, you know, I'll hear something and it just moves me, just music. Just music. It doesn't have to be jazz or anything in particular, just music. Yeah.
Of course there was no jazz when you first started. I mean there wasn't -- there was jazz but it wasn't around you I'm sure.
Well, oh, yes, it was. Oh, on the contrary, sure it was. I was aware of all different types of music, as I was coming up, you see. I came up in New York,
right down there on 64th Street, where I grew up, right here on 64th Street, between Amsterdam and West End. We used to call it the jungles.
Yeah, right.

And just those four or five blocks where the blacks lived in those days, you know, in that concentration, it was a hotbed of jazz and blues and everything else. I mean they publicized Harlem, but Harlem wasn't Harlem then. It was all down there where I was born, you know. And that's where the -- they used to call them the house rent parties and all that, and I remember very distinctly we'd go to bed at night and of course everything would be quiet and all you would hear was these piano players, all up and down the street, playing the blues and the boogie-woogie and all that stuff, you know. In later years, you know, they liked to credit this to Kansas City and this to this place and this to that place, but it had always gone on right here in New York.
It was.

Sure. Sure it was. Now, and this is in World War I I'm talking about. So naturally it was going on before that. Plus I remember in my house, you know, we always had a piano and instruments laying around, you know. My brother studied a little trumpet afterward, my oldest brother, he studied a little trumpet later on, and my father used to have friends and almost -- I wouldn't say almost all of the, but a
whole lot of friends of my father's, they'd come in the house and jump right on the piano and start playing the piano, you know. Like what they call stride piano. Stride piano's New York piano.
Right.
Stride piano is New York piano. I never heard it anywhere else but New York.
That's right. That's what they always say.

Fats Waller, Willy "the Lion", James B. [P.] Johnson, right on down the line. Corky -- there used to be a whole lot who never got much publicity, but a whole lot of them. They played stride piano. That's New York piano.
They always refer to James A. Johnson as the father of stride piano. Was he really the first? Weren't there others?

No. You know they put these names on people. You can't say who is who or what is what, way back to Scott Joplin. What the hell, I mean, you know, all these guys, they played, one copied from the other and the other copied from -- even now you have Fats Waller on a record and you're not sure it's Fats, you know. You say, "Yeah, that's Fats," and then you had Jimmy Johnson, you know. You know, playing about along the same lines. But out of all those piano players, you know, I like Willy "the Lion's" style. You know, he plays that delicate
sort of (Imitating piano). You know, that style. He plays a lot of things. Plus, he can -- look here, Willis "the Lion" plays "Carolina Shout," man, that's the classic all time great, you know. Yeah.
Now, you -- now, what is this about Lieutenant Eugene Mikell and the 369th [Street] Cadets?
Oh, I was growing up then. I wasn't growing up, but that was after I -- I was about --
Would you like to take that and put it behind you?

Yeah, yeah. That's a good idea, yeah. I was about -- put it like this. Yeah. Yeah. Nice. Thanks. At that time, you see, I had -- I never could remember whether this was before -- well, when I was about 14 or 15 years old I discovered Fletcher Henderson's band, because I went to a dance. Fletcher Henderson was playing at the Roseland Ballroom, Roseland Ballroom in New York, and so all these clubs, you know, these colored clubs, used to give these big dances and they used to give dances at the Renaissance Casino. The Savoy wasn't built yet. The Renaissance Casino, the Star Casino, wherever, uptown, so Fletcher used to get -- they used to hire Fletcher as an attraction and he'd come uptown and play an hour after his Roseland date. Then they'd advertise Fletcher Henderson, and there were big crowds, you know. And the house band was John C. Smith. You know he had a sedate band. They just played

stock arrangements, you know, till Fletcher got there, then he'd turn on the jazz. So anyhow, so you know, young kids, we went to this dance. It cost $1.10 to go to the dance. So we saved our money and we went to the dance.
That was a lot of money then, wasn't it?

Oh, yeah, $1.10. It took you all day -- it took you all month to get $1.10. My mother used to give us a dollar to go to the store and come back with a bag of groceries this high for $1.10, $1.25, you know. Well, anyhow, I -- well, we, I'd say -- we were there, because Louis Armstrong was getting real famous. Everybody was talking about him. In those days we called him Fats Armstrong. Fats Armstrong. You know, Coleman Hawkins, and we'd heard the records. So anyway, I went to this dance and I heard Fletcher Henderson's band, and I just stood there with my mouth open all night. I didn't move away from the front of the bandstand. Oh, I never heard anything like that in my life. And I think right then I decided what I was going to do with my life. Right then. You couldn't tell me anything about school, you couldn't tell me anything about work, or anything. That was it. From then on I just dreamed, you know, music, and --
Was this when Louis was with the band?
Yeah.
This was when he was with it?
Yeah. Yeah, Louis was with the band. This was in 19 --
Must have been '25 or so.

I think it was before that. No, it was before '25. Louis was with --well, anyway, Louis was with it. I just read Max Jones' book about Louis Armstrong a couple of weeks ago. Louis was only with Fletcher about a year, was it?
Yeah, a short time.
A very short time.
13 mos.
A very short time.
Yeah, well, anyway, he was with it. What year was it, '24?
It was --
Well, it was '25, then, whatever it was. Whatever it was. So -- well, it ties in about this Mikell, Mikell, yeah, that's what Stanley Dance's name is. We used to call him Michael.
Oh.
I don't know why everybody called him -- we used to call him Professor Michael, or Lieutenant.
Well, wasn't it spelled M-i-k-e-l-1?
Yeah.
Yeah.

Well, we still said Michael. And now his son -- I went to school with his son Gene. Gene, he was a musician, he played with the Mills Blue Rythm Band at the Cotton Club, and he had an older brother, Otto Mikell. He was a saxophone player too. He played saxophone and cello. He died recently over in Montclair, New Jersey. And, well, I don't want to stray. Getting back to the -- but then this Mikell, he started the 369th Cadet Boys Band, see. He got the idea to, because he was the band leader of the 15th Regiment Band after Jim Europe was killed.
Oh.

See, then he took over the band. He was a Lieutenant. So then -- so it tied in. So I said to him, I said, "Well, I can't join the band. I'm a violin player. I can't march with a violin." So he says, "Well, I tell you what. There's clarinet players that we need," and he said, "Would you like to play?" I said, "Oh, yeah," because I'd seen Buster Bailey up there with this clarinet. Buster Bailey was one of my heroes, and he still is, because I think Buster Bailey, regardless of what anyone says about Buster Bailey Buster Bailey was the best clarinet player I ever knew. And I wouldn't care what you say about anybody. He's the best. Whatever -- of course I mean everybody can't do everything, you know.
But the first time you heard Buster
was with Henderson.

Oh, yes. Oh, yes, yes, yes. So I -- so then I went to my father. I said -- now, I've been taking violin lessons now about eight, nine, ten years. Steady, studying the violin, you know. I played in the high school orchestra up on 66th Street, used to be Commerce High School, and we won first prize in greater New York, the school orchestra, and I was one of the first violin players, you know. So my father, he couldn't hear of that, you know. He was of that old school, you know, he'd say, "What do you mean, buy you a clarinet?" And he told me no. "No," he said, "I'm not going to buy you no clarinet." But my dear mother was always in the background. She says -- so, lo and behold, I got a clarinet and started, you know, taking clarinet lessons, and again I'd say I liked it. I liked it too. I liked the clarinet. So about -- you know, so I started digging with those -- you know, we played simple marches, not the big time stuff like Washington Post" and all that. Not that hard stuff. We played, you know, sort of simple marches, kids, you know. So I got along on the clarinet pretty good. So then there was a -- so all the kids up and down the street, you know, some of them had saxophones, they had trumpets and trombones, and almost every kid you used to see on the street in those days had some kind of instrument in his hand. A violin or trumpet or, you know. So we all used to meet. Some kids had drums, you know, we'd meet and try to
play a little music, a little jazz or whatever. So I used to take this kid's saxophone, you know.

So about a couple years later, Christmas, and my mother told me, she says, "Go look in the closet over there. There's something in there for you." And I looked in there and there's a brand new saxophone and a case and --
: Alto sax?
Yeah. So I got the -- well, that's how I got started in the --
: Were there any other of those kids that stayed with the music that we might know of?
Yes. You know Freddy Jenkins who used to play with -- well, he was in this high school orchestra.
: Oh, he was.

Yeah. Won the prize, and there's some who didn't. Benny Carter was along. Benny, he didn't go to the same school I did, and he didn't play in this orchestra, but he was along about that same time, and another fellow named Farley Jordan, he was a trombone player. He played a little bit professional. And there was a few of them who played, you know, professionally. Not -- they never got too big, but they played. They could play.
: Now, your first professional job, was that the Willy Freeman?
Oh, Willy Freeman. What have you been
(Laughs)

reading? Willy Freeman, I'd completely -- well, see, Willy Freeman, he was going to Commerce High School, and he was a violin player, and he had what they call a -- they call them -- well, he just had a local band uptown. He lived up on -- oh, I don't know, 136th Street or 137th Street, someplace. And he used to have -- he used to get these local jobs, you know, and he had a set band that he'd play these local gigs with, and then he -- then when he met me, I met him when I was in high school, and he met me, so he invited me up to rehearsal, and so I got to get in that band and play some of the gigs they had, you know. And it was a great thing, because then it was like I was discovering something, you know, and in those days we used to get -- you'd play a job, like up to the Renaissance Casino. You know where the Renaissance Casino is. I mean we played -- we got $12.00. Twelve whole dollars for playing, you know, these few hours. I said wow, this is going to be great, you know.
Now, this was what, around 1926? Would that be right?
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Now, what sort of music did Willy Freeman's band play?
Well, they had stock arrangements. They played stock arrangements. We played stock arrangements, because there wasn't any money to have special arrangements
made and that sort of thing.
So did that leave any room for solos, or was that strictly reading?

Oh, mostly, I think, we were reading everything, yeah, which was a good education for me, because I knew my music, you know, but I just had to make the transition, you know, the adjustment on a saxophone, you know.
So with Freeman you were already playing saxophone.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I had to. I had to play saxophone.
Were you doubling on clarinet?
Yeah. Yeah.
Now, what about Campbell, the drummer, Jimmy Campbell. Was that --

Yes, Jimmy Campbell. He was a fellow out of Brooklyn. He was a drummer, and I don't remember just how I got in contact with him. But it was a summer job, up in Albany, at this roadhouse. You know, they used to call them roadhouses in those days. They were out of town and of course this was during prohibition, and they sold bootleg whiskey and the gangsters. I think it was -- it was a gangster house, of course it was. I remember the fellow who owned it was an old Irishman named Ames O'Brien, yeah, and so we played up there with him. We had how many pieces? A drummer, a piano player, a
guitar player and myself, four pieces. Yeah. Then later on, we added another piece. We added Johnny Russell. Did you ever hear of Johnny Russell, a tenor player?
Yeah.
Then we got him and he came up there and played.
Now, was this still playing stock arrangements?

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, we -- that's what it was. We had a -- and the piano player, what was his name? His name was Paddy somebody. He was an elderly fellow. Oh, I don't know if I should say older fellow, because he'd been playing, you know, professionally around New York for quite awhile, and he -- you know, he sort of had control of the band and he -- in other words the kind of fellow you could learn a lot from and I learned a lot from him and he could play those charts good, you know, and tell you, you know, this goes like that, you know, and all that sort of thing.
Now, at this point --
Paddy Armstead, his name was, yeah.
At this point in time a lot of jazz records have started coming out. Louis' 'Hot Five'. Henderson records and so forth.
Oh, Henderson's records were out before that.
Oh, yes, sure.
Oh, yeah.
By 1926 they're --
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
And there's a lot of jazz being recorded.
Yeah.
So did that -- was that very meaningful to you, to a musician at that time, or did you listen to a lot of records?
Oh, yeah, yeah.
And learn from them, or --

Oh, yes, of course. Of course. I remember those records. They used to cost 75 cents. And I used to buy them. I used to buy a record -- I used to go in a store and ask the man, "Do you have any Louis Armstrong records?" And he'd say yeah, and I'd just buy it. I wouldn't even listen to it. Louis Armstrong, good enough for me, I'd just buy it. Fletcher Henderson records, yeah. And everybody -- I wouldn't say anybody, but most people's houses, you know, you went to, had Fletcher Henderson's records. They could say what they want about all these people nowadays, but I never got the figures, I never saw them published anywhere, but Fletcher Henderson must have sold a hell of a lot of records. Somebody made a hell of a lot of money.
: Yes, right.

That's right, you believe that. Because everywhere -- not I lived in 99th Street, right down here, later on, after I moved from 64th Street, after we moved, I should say, and we lived in 99th Street. I started playing these Louis Armstrong records, and in about six months the whole damned neighborhood was playing Louis Armstrong and Fletcher Henderson's records. That's right. Educated the whole neighborhood. That's right.
: What about -- when did you start going to -- the Lafayette Theater was running then and having shows.
Yeah.
: Did you start going to catch the shows in Harlem?
Oh, yes, of course. My mother and father used to take us to the Lafayette when I was --
: Do you remember them?

Sure. Sure. Well, you see, the accent wasn't on bands and music. There were a few people, like there was a -- what was his name? What was this trumpet player's name? A real popular jazz trumpet player. Johnny Dunn.
: Johnny Dunn, yes.
Then there's another trumpet player named Jack Hatton. You never heard of him.
: No.

Well, anyway, he's one of those that used to come out with a derby and a hat and anything, and the bottles and make all kinds of sounds and noises and -- it was jazz he was playing, and at that time those were the people, mostly, who were featured. Because there -- it wasn't the thing to have jazz bands on the stage. All those vaudeville houses had bands in the pit.
: Yeah.

You know, and the pit bands would give a little stab at some sort of jazz every now and then, and you know, in concert with whatever was on the stage, maybe, because all the acts were black acts, mostly. Every once in awhile they'd have a, you know, white act or something, a ventriloquist or -- what do you call these acts? You know, a bicycle act or acrobat -- acrobat I'm trying to say, yeah. And -- but the pit bands stuck strictly to that music. You know, they'd have an overture before the show, you know. But then gradually the jazz part of it and the bands, the big bands, crept into it, you know, that instead of a show they just featured bands. But that came later on, and what used to be featured was five and six piece jazz bands, you know. Like in the Lafayette you're speaking of. Well, that's the way it was, and that's where I first heard Duke's band.
: At the Lafayette?
No, at the Lincoln.
Oh.
Do you know where the Lincoln Theater was? It's a church now.
Yes. Fats Waller used to play there.

Yeah. Yeah. And that's where I heard -- at the Lincoln Theater -- or was it the Lafayette? Either the Lincoln or the Lafayette, Fats was playing organ, and Fats used to play -- Fats was playing the organ, then the pit band came on. Then they played together, the organ and the pit band, and that was one of the most beautiful sounds I'd ever heard up till then. I never heard a band and an organ play together. And, oh, that was beautiful, beautiful, you know. Because, you know, Fats, he could really play. He -- yeah. Yeah.
That was probably at the Lincoln, then, where he used to play the organ.
Is that where he used to play?
Yeah.
Probably the Lincoln, yeah. Well, incidentally, the Lincoln stage was the first stage I was ever on, the Lincoln.
Oh. How did that happen?
I played -- did you ever hear of Lucille Hagamin?
Sure. I recorded her.
Oh, you did?
Yeah.

Yeah. Well, Lucille Hagan, she had an act patterned after Mamie Smith and everybody else, a blues act, you know, and you know, like, "Aggravatin' Papa, Don't You Two-Time Me," and all that stuff. She's a nice looking light-complected woman, you know.
She's been up here.
Yeah. Yeah. Is she still around?
No, she died a few years ago.

Oh, too bad. The last time I saw her was -- there's a men's club called the -- what do they call it, the Old Timers or -- no, the Boys of Yesteryear, and I went to that dance with -- I was off one night. This was while I was working with Duke and I went up there, and lo and behold she was up there and I got to see her again. That's the last time I saw her.
Yeah. I recorded her with Willie "the Lion" Smith.
Oh, yeah?
With Willie accompanying her and Buster on baritone.
Buster Bailey. Oh, good.
In 1961. But how was that that you came to -- when was this you performed with her?

Well, this was all in the same time -- oh, this was shortly after I started playing. It must have been about 1926. See, in those times a whole lot happened in one year, jumping around from here to there to there to there. And I always tried to advance myself, everytime I'd make a move it was with a better group, you know. Yeah. The Lincoln Theater.
Do you remember -- did you ever hear Bessie Smith work?
No.
At the Lafayette, or --

Look, I may have. I wouldn't say I hadn't, I didn't. I may have, but there was so much going on. There were so many people around in those days that I probably heard her. But I remember distinctly hearing Ma Rainey, because Ma Rainey was pretty popular in those days, and she was coming to the Lafayette and there was talk, you know, for about a month before she got there. I said, 'Gee, whiz, Ma Rainey must be terrific. I've got to hear her,' you know. And I went to hear her and to tell you the truth I wasn't too impressed with her. She's a big, fat ugly chick.
Known as the ugliest woman in show business.
Well, she was named right. She was almost as ugly as this chick out of Chicago used to sing the

blues. What was that other chick's name? Well, I can't remember all these names. But anyhow, you know, in those days, now Mamie Smith, she got pretty big. I picked up a couple of her records, and I only bought her records because Louis Armstrong was with them. Clarence Williams and somebody else. Somebody gave them to me or something. I don't think I bought them.

Anyway, but in those days, you know, at the Lafayette they were real great, you know. Everything was happening because everything had to happen right there, because in those days, you know, there wasn't much action for the black bands and black artists and all that, downtown.
Right.
There was just a few, Fletcher Henderson was working at Roseland.
There was a place called Jungle Casino, with James P. Johnson.
I don't know that place. I don't remember that.
That is supposedly where the Charleston started. People from Charleston, South Carolina used to hang out at the Jungle Casino.
I don't know that story. I don't know.
What about Greenwich Village? Weren't there -- or was that earlier in the (Unintelligible).
Well, I'll tell you, that gets back
to the history, to the history of Manhattan Island and New York City. Now, actually, you know, Harlem isn't as old as people think it is.
Right.

Right. You know, if you know the history like I said before. When I grew up on 64th Street, Harlem wasn't -- Harlem went from 130th Street to 145th Street, from 130th to 140th Street, or something like that. And from 5th Avenue to 8th Avenue, if that far. So it was just a few blocks.
The Apollo Theater was a Jewish, Yiddish theater.

Yeah, of course. Of course. Yeah, well, you know, so that was it. So all the black people lived all over. They lived at 33rd Street, 23rd Street, down in the Village. You know, up and down Broadway, 8th Avenue, 3rd Avenue on the east side. You know, it was like that. Then what happened to the black people, Harlem -- Harlem, for some reason or other, then they began renting these places to the colored people, so naturally that was a status symbol to live in Harlem. So all the people down where I lived, they'd say, 'Oh, yeah, we're moving up in Harlem.' So that's how that happened.
Yeah.
So like you asked me about the Village, the Village is -- and I remember I used to get jobs down in the
village, you know, about the time I told you I started, about the time when Lucille HaggU.min and Willy Freeman and I used to get a job every now and then down in the Village, you know.
Well, where does the 116th Street Dancing School come in?

That's Willy Martineau. That's Willy Martineau's band. Willy Martineau was a -- that was in 1927. In 1927, the year Lindbergh flew across the ocean. Yeah. Yeah, because I was working there when he flew across the ocean. Never will forget that. Took him 33 hours. Well, anyway, I was in this -- I remember I was home. I lived at 99th Street. I lived at 47 West 99th Street then, and this fellow, Charlie Madsen -- I'd never had a job like that, you know, a job where you go to work every night, every night, every night, every night. So I was home about a couple of weeks, you know, and I was still rehearsing with the kids in the block, you know, and I used to play basketball at St. Cyprims Church on 63rd Street, and incidentally, that's where I was baptized.

So this particular day Charlie Madsen -- and he was a pretty good booking agent, because he was the guy who booked Fletcher Henderson. And he called me up. I said, 'Ooh, wow, great.' So he said, 'Well, there's a job open at the Dancing School.' You know, would I like to -- I said, 'Oh, fine, yes, of course.' So we went to work there at -- it was the Parody. The name of it was the Parody, Parody of ballrooms. It was just
a dancing school, you know, a dime a dance.
Right.
We played from 8:00 to 12:00.
Oh, so it wasn't really a school.
Well, they called it a dancing -- it was a dancing school. See, the girl's -- they had these girls there. Officially they were teaching the customers to dance.
I see.

But actually they were doing everything but teach, you know. Yeah. So we'd play -- the dances were very short. You played a chorus, a chorus and a half, and every time the music stopped they'd give a ticket. Well, that's the way it was. And I worked there a year and a half, see, and it was good because I got a chance to learn and play and you know, -- it was four or five pieces. Two saxophones, trumpet, drums and piano, five pieces. We worked there a year and a half.
And again you were just playing arrangements, huh?
Oh, we played stocks.
Yeah. But had you at this point started -- I mean had you only played arrangements up to that point? Did you ever start -- had you started improvising yet?
Oh, of course.
Where?
I don't know. I guess I'd started that stuff when I first picked up the clarinet.
Oh, when you -- yeah, I mean in a job, though.

Well, I was doing that, I mean -- that sort of came naturally to me. You know, I'd play my lessons, my exercises -- you see, I had known from studying the violin the procedure. Like you had to play your exercises. Then you had a book. You had two books -- I'm talking about on the violin -- you had two books. You had a book for technique and exercises, and then you had another book with melodies, simple melodies, selections from this opera and from this classical, you know, composition or whatever, and then you played that too. And you had to have -- the two of them went together, so that's the way you'd advance. So when I got the clarinet I followed the same pattern, only instead of the classical -- the classical, I tried to play some blues or a chorus I'd heard Buster play or all these people who were -- like Boyd Senter. Remember Boyd Senter?
Sure.

And Ted Lewis and Johnny Dodds, and whoever, Frank Signorelli, people with the original Memphis Five or the Dixieland Jazz Band. See, my father used to buy all these records. And I'd play them at home and listen to them. Then I'd try to play them. So by the time I got to

Willy Martineau, I was with this fellow who played tenor, his name was Wheat, Bubba Wheat. Yes, Bubba Wheat. He's in Florida now. He just called me up about a couple of years ago and gave me his clarinet, said he's through playing. Well, he'd worked a long time on -- he went to sea, you know, so he never got big, but at that time he had played in shows, you know. He used to play the blues. He was a great blues player, you know, and I learned a lot of the blues from him, you know. I picked up, you know.
Were there a lot of good musicians who we never heard of because they just dropped out?

Oh, yes. A whole lot of them. A whole lot of them. There was a kid around there -- well, I call him a kid, he was older than I was, his name was Freddie Welch. He was a clarinet player. And there was another fellow named Bob Fuller, a clarinet player. And I --
Bob Fuller, he made some records.
I think he did, yeah.
With Elmer Snowden.
Yeah.
And Bessie Smith, I think.

See, there was a whole lot of places to play in those days. Like I said before, in Harlem there was about -- oh, there must have been a dozen, 15, 20 what they used to call big bands in those days. A big band was 11, 12

pieces, they called a big band, you know. And there were untold amounts of combos, two pieces, three pieces, four pieces. Almost every doorway you'd pass you'd hear some music coming out, a piano or something. Of course in those days there were a lot of buffet flats, because you remember the prohibition.
Yeah, right.
Buffet flats.
Were there certain places where musicians used to hang out?
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
Where?

One -- there used to be musicians' clubs, and one place was called the Band Box. The Band Box was on 131st Street, off of 7th Avenue. Then later on the Rhythm Club, the Rhythm Club. But these places were what you call famous, we called famous, because everybody in Harlem, and the people from downtown used to come uptown in those days and frequent these places, you know, because

in those days nobody was afraid to go anywhere. You'd see these people from downtown with high silk hats and the ladies in diamonds and furs and things, and just strolling down the street, you know, 3:00 or 4:00 o'clock in the morning, you know.
Now, what about Sapiro ?
Sapiro.
Sapiro . you called him.
Sapiro.

Well, he was from New Orleans, you know. He was supposed to be a -- what do you call them? A Cajun or whatever, I don't know. We called him Henry Sapiro back then. If you saw him you'd think he was I don't know what, you know, dressed very fine, and he had his hair all combed on the side. Well, that was really the first time that I played in a band that had a book with special arrangements.
Oh.
And they had one or two of Fletcher Henderson's arrangements.

Jimmy Arche y.

Uh-huh.
Yeah, that was a real --

The Bamboo Inn?
Yeah. Yeah. It -- so then they came --

Rose Danceland, was that a dancing school, like the 116th Street Dancing School?
Yeah. Yeah. Only it was on a higher level. It was more elaborate and bigger, more girls, and a bigger band and everything, you know, on a larger scale.
Where was it located?
125th Street and 7th Avenue. You know where that cigar store is?
Yes.
The cigar store's still there. It was right upstairs, over that. Yeah.
So it was right next to the -- it was near -- next to the Alhambra.
Yeah. Well, the Alhambra's on the corner of 126th Street.
Yeah.
Yeah.
But that block, the same block.
Yeah. Yeah. I worked the Alhambra too. I worked there with Chick Webb.
But -- okay, so you -- how long were you there, at Rose Danceland?
Oh, how long was I there? My time, you know, gets -- I forget.
Well, I have it that you were with Charlie Skeets in '27 and that you worked with Jelly Roll Morton in the summer of '28. So would that be part of '27 and into '28?
Yeah, I guess so, yeah.
Now, when you worked with Jelly Roll, was he already a name known to you when you went in?

No. Not really. I'd probably heard his name, but he didn't -- I mean the name didn't mean too much to me at that time. I was just discovering all these people and this music, I just discovered, you know, what it meant and what they were playing, because at that time I was more steeped in what was happening right here in New York, and as I discovered these people -- you know, like it was -- mostly what happened was, you know, like you say, the musicians' club, you know, all these older musicians, they sit around and talk like about Chicago and wherever, and I listened, and like they used to talk about Joe Oliver and Johnny St.Cyr. and all those old guys, you know --
Well, they weren't really that old then.
Huh?
They weren't really that old then.

Well, they were older than I was, you know. I don't know how old -- I was about 17, 18, 19. They were probably 25. I called them old, you know. Yeah. So anyway, when I discovered Jelly Roll, you know, he -- I realized that he really had something, you know, his style and his music and his -- and I have one record home now I made with Jelly Roll. I was just playing it last week. I made it in must have been '28, '28 when I --
What was that?
"Red Hot Pepper Stomp," or something.
Well, I can't imagine Jelly Roll playing stock arrangements.

Well, in the dancing school, see, in the dancing school you played so much you had to play stock arrangements. See, you played -- the schedule in most dancing schools was you played 50 minutes and would rest 10, or 55 minutes and rest 5. You know, because if you had to get off the bandstand you just got off. Or if you wanted a sandwich, you just got off and got your sandwich, you know, or something like that, but the music was continuous, continuous, so of course you couldn't have special arrangements like that. And you played stock arrangements, stock arrangements, and --
It just seems so strange, because
at that point Jelly Roll had already accomplished quite a bit. He'd made a lot of records. For him to -- you would -- one would think he was too big to take a job like that at that stage.

Well, I often wondered about that, but I figured he -- Jelly Roll was a sort of an up and down guy, you know, like he would be in the chips now and six months from then he would be down. Because -- which I suppose was -- you could attribute to his personality, his inability to get along too good with people, as they say. Jelly Roll was a battler, you know, an old school fighter. He used to tell stories, you know. I hadn't paid too much attention to them. But at that time Jelly Roll was sort of gruff, you know, a gruff sort of fellow. He -- and up to that time he was the only fellow who ever fired me, see.
Really?

Oh, yeah. So one night he made a statement. He says -- because in the band, you know, we were sort of reluctant to listen to him, because he came and he was going to take over the band, and so we sort of resented that, you know. I suppose we thought that one of us should have been the lead, you know. So he came up there with his pictures. The man had his picture outside and all that. So one night he came to work and he said, 'Well, I'm going to either run this band or break it up.' Something like that, you know. So I told him, I said, 'Well, it looks like you're

going to have to break it up. So he said -- so one word led to another, anyway, so he fired me. I only stayed fired a week. He called me up and told me to come on back to work, you know. So we became all right, you know. What is that?
Videotape in the tape recorder.
But I remember he operated on a big -- on a big level, you know.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, he did, you know, and he brought a broadcasting wire in there. You know, we used to broadcast on -- we had a matinee on Sunday and we used to broadcast the Sunday matinee.
And Jelly Roll arranged that?
Yeah. I remember he made an arrangement on 'Tiger Rag.' He made an arrangement on a couple of other things we used to play, his music.
Was he at that time bragging as much as he did later on?
That's what I said, yeah.
That he invented the music and all that?
No, he said he invented jazz.
He was saying that even then.
Oh, yes, sure. That's what he said, yeah.
Well, how did people react to that? Did people take him seriously?

Well, he -- he had an audience then, I will say that. He had an audience then. But he didn't get to -- he wasn't at his best up in this dancing school, because most of the people came there, they couldn't care less, you know, who was playing the music. They just came there to dance. They didn't even look at the musicians hardly. And Jelly Roll -- of course Jelly Roll went on and what he did, he had all these big ideas, and his idea was to take the band out of this dancing school and go out on the road, and I never heard of such a thing. You know. That's what he did. You know. We went down in Pennsylvania, in the coal country, you know, all around in -- that was good dance territory in those days. But that didn't last long, because most of the fellows that were in the band, they didn't want to travel that way, you know. They didn't want to travel.
Well, what sort of places did you play at?
Just dance halls.
Dance halls.
Dance halls. Dance halls. Every town had a dance hall and every town had a band.
And it was called Jelly Roll Morton's orchestra?
Jelly Roll Morton and his Red Hot Peppers.
Oh, it was the Red Hot Peppers.
His Red Hot Peppers.
And was it during that period that you recorded with him?
Yeah. Yeah.
In Camden.
No, we recorded in New York.
In New York.

Yeah. I just had the 78 at home. I've got it home. But you see, Jelly Roll, he had these big ideas which are very good, and during the time we were playing at the Rose Danceland, he imported Omer Simeon from New York and there's another clarinet player named Blue. Blue was from St. Louis. And --
You mean Omer Simeon he imported from New Orleans.
Well, he was in Chicago at the time.
Oh, he was in Chicago.

He was originally from New Orleans, but he came up to Chicago. And he had Paul Barbarin. He was on his way to, you know, build up something, you know. Then the only thing -- there's one thing I always regretted. Then he started rehearsing the band up at the Renaissance, and
he was supposed to take this band in the Roseland, see. Rose Danceland and Roseland is two different places.
Right.

And this band he was rehearsing, he had Omer Sim?on, Barney Bigard and myself in the reed section. And who were the trumpets? He had a fellow named -- I can't remember, I can see him, but I can't remember the name. Paul Barbarin was on drums. Oh, I can't remember the names. But I always thought that if that had of gotten off the ground, you know, I would have liked that very much, because the people he had in the band were great jazz players, like Omer Simeon and Barney Bigard and I think he had Louis Metcalf on trumpet, and -- I can see the guy right now. I can't think of his name. (probably Ward Pinkett) Anyway --
But he wrote the arrangements himself.
Oh, yes.
And they were very -- were they more imaginative than most arrangements in that time?

Yeah. Yeah. If he had been able to get it to going and get this job and get to playing on this job, I believe he would have had one of the great bands. Because it was all there. It just didn't get off the ground.
When was the last time you saw Jelly Roll?
Oh, when was the last time? Just to

show you now, when I was playing down at the Onyx Club with John Kirby, 52nd Street, I saw Jelly Roll down there, and he came in a few nights and played, and played the piano, you know, while -- I guess he was just scrounging around trying to find a job someplace. And he played like sort of relief piano. When we'd get off the stand he'd play. But I think that's one of the -- when did he die?
He died -- I'm trying to remember -- the very early '40s, maybe even '41 or 2.*
Yeah. Yeah. It was about that. Well, this, what I'm talking about, is about '39.

I guess so, yeah.

Was that -- was that considered at that time, for instance when you were asked to do the first record, was that a very exciting thing, or was that just another job?
Well, it was just another job. I would say -- well, at that time -- how can I put it? As I remember I wasn't too excited, because it was a --
You weren't the leader, for one thing.
Oh, no. Oh, no, no.
So, there was no disc jockey in those days, so you didn't expect the record to bring in more work, I would imagine.

Well, actually, see, it's a funny thing. All during my career, I mean people always ask me questions. It wasn't -- my ambitions weren't along those lines. I wouldn't think -- because in the first place I was home when I was --

you know, with my family, my parents and all that. And I -- and what I was doing wasn't gaited to eating and sleeping. I was doing it because I loved it. And right not, till today, I mean money isn't my prime object, you know. Of course I mean I'd hate to be without money, but what I mean is it wasn't -- and I think people who do that, there's something missing in their -- you know, in their liking for what they do. Now, like you say about the record date, it was just another place to play, you know, and the record came out, you know, and I'd listen to it and say, "Well." And right now, today, if I make a record today, you know, I listen to it, and I say -- and I never made a record that I didn't think if I made it over again I could do it better. Never. Uh-huh. Now, after the Rose Dance-land, did you then go to Benny Carter?
That's where I went after Rose Danceland?

Well, that's all I have. Maybe I left something out in the middle, maybe I didn't. But I have it that in the summer of '28 you were with Rose Danceland, and Morton, and then you went to Benny Carter's band in '29, sometime, at the Arcadia.

Well, you see, there's a break there, in the -- Christmas, 1928, I was out in Detroit with McKinney's Cotton Pickers. I went out there and -- hand me that envelope there, please. Oh, uh-huh.
So I refer to this.
To refresh (Inaudible) your memory.

I'll tell you, there was so much going on at one time.
Yeah. Fast and furious. You know, you'd stay on a job about two months, you know, and go to

Oh, yeah?
Yeah.

(Greystone)
Yeah, I know which one you mean.
You know what I mean, yeah. And the reason I didn't stay was because that job closed and they were

I got there Christmas Day, for Christmas Day, 1928. I never will forget that, because the first time I'm away from home for Christmas, you know, and I'm sitting up in this coffee shop, eating ham and eggs, and they're playing Christmas carols, and the tears were running down my eyes. And I said, "What the hell am I doing out here in Detroit?" So I had a lot of fun, but I came back to New York. Then it was after that that I joined Benny Carter and jobs were always closing, and Benny's job closed too. And we were supposed to -- Benny's band -- and they closed about a month or two after I had joined his band, and the band supposedly was supposed to go back into the Arcadia Ballroom, but they never did.
What was the Arcadia like?

Well, it was on the order of the Roseland Ballroom, but it was built entirely different. It was larger than the Roseland Ballroom and had a stage like -- I don't know whether it had a stage and a balcony that ran around. I don't know whether it was a theater that was, you know, converted into a ballroom or whatever. Anyway, it was a ballroom at that time, and they had two bands, you know. They had two stages, one on each stage.
Alternating.
Yeah. Well, Roseland too had two bands. But then after that, after -- after Benny Carter's band, where did I go?
Well, you were with Chick Webb, weren't you?

Yeah, I guess I did. I think I -- see, like I was getting fairly into the business then and I think I just gigged around for a couple of months or so. Because the business was good at that time. You could leave one job and go on another job or just freelance around with different people. There was a guy named Peekaboo Jimmy. Peekaboo Jimmy was a drummer, and he was a -- and he'd see you and he'd say, 'Well, I've got some gigs for you and he'd take out your book and he'd write all these jobs down, a half a dozen jobs, you know. You played in places like the Bamboo Inn, you know, this was all during Prohibition, and people brought their own liquor there and everybody was selling bootleg liquor there. Were you ever in places that were raided?

No, that's one thing, all my career, I was never in a place that was raided, never. They used to raid the -- in fact they'd raid most anyplace when they got ready. Even the Musicians' Club they used to raid. On any trumped up excuse, because they used to have gambling in the back room and all that. The Musicians' Club always had
gambling. They had poker tables and blackjack tables and whatever. But I was never in a room that was raided.
What about the buffet flats, what were they like?

Well, a buffet flat was where you went to eat, drink. Some of them were bawdy houses, you know. And it could be any house, a house like this, an apartment. An apartment, an apartment like this. And the standing joke was you could go in almost any apartment house and knock on almost any door and get something to drink, you know. You'd knock on the door and they'd say, "Who's there?" "Jimmy sent me." You know, okay, and he'd crack the door and look at you, and the thing I always marveled at -- I went through too, I used to do it, knock on the door, and he'd say to you, "What do you want, a pint?" You'd say yeah, and whatever he gave you you took. Whatever. You didn't specify anything in particular. Then later on the drink that became popular was shakeup gin, they used to call it. They used to have this gin, and I suppose the gangsters used to put it up. Of course you wouldn't get this in the average apartment, but it used to be -- the bottle used to say Gordon's Gin. It was wrapped up in yellow paper, you know. It cost one buck. Gordon's Gin.
What about some of the other entertainers? Do you remember -- well, Gladys Bentley, for instance?
Yes, I worked with Gladys Bentley. I
worked with Gladys Bentley down at the --
The Ubangi?
The Ubangi Club. That was after Fletcher Henderson.
What was the Ubangi like?

The Ubangi was the old Connie's Inn. It was a nice room for a nightclub, but it was built for -- I suppose it was built to be a nightclub, because it had a dance floor and bandstand and it had lights all around, you know, the floor. And they too served Chinese food.
That was very common in those days, wasn't it?
Yeah.
To have jazz in places where they had Chinese food. Were they called chop suey joints?
No. No, not these places, no. No. It was just Connie's Inn.
Uh-huh. Now Gladys, did she always wear tails and pants?
Yeah, that was her --
That was her thing.
That was her thing, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
I always found that interesting that you have -- you have female impersonators, but you don't have male impersonators today.
No.
But in those days there were several of them.
Yeah. Yeah.
She wasn't the only one, Gladys Bentley.
No. No. Oh, yeah --
There was another Gladys at that time up there. Gladys Ferguson.
I don't remember her.
Don't you?
No. There was another one. She was a singer, too. I can't remember her name, but she used to work -- she used to work around Harlem. Yeah. Gladys Bentley.
Did you ever work in any of the shows?

No. No. I never wanted to do anything on that order. I didn't want to just sit there and play a show. That wasn't my thing, you know. I didn't want to do that at all. Although I liked it. I suppose I liked it because I just heard it once or twice. But to have a steady diet of the same thing, night after night after night, I don't think I would like that. Of course we used to play shows. The only shows I played was like at the Apollo, I did stock, what they call it, in the Apollo, with -- again, I can't remember names. I did stock in the Apollo for about a month. But that was too hard
because you had to rehearse next week's show while you were playing this week's show, and that became too much. It was too confining, you know. So I quit that.
Did you ever play the old Cotton Club?
No. No. Well, yeah, I played in there a few times with just a fill-in band, you know, somebody to play up there awhile, to be the house band, that was off somewhere.
Now, did they not allow black people in there, customers, or did they just discourage them? Was there an actual rule?

Well, I don't know. I don't know whether to say it was -- discouraged them, I would say, I suppose, it was. Like I would say yes. But I don't -- I don't think they allowed them up there. No, I would say they wouldn't, no. But I went up there a few times, you know. I went up there a few times to see the show, you know.
So you could come in because you were a performer?

Well, I don't know whether they knew I was a performer or not, you know. I just walked in, you know, right straight in the front door and straight up the steps, you know. They had booths. It was a fairly nice place. I'd go there they had a band. I went there with Duke. I went there with Cab and whoever was there, you know.
What about Small's?

Oh, Small's was the first cabaret I was ever in. That was when Small's was on 5th Avenue, 5th Avenue and 35th Street was Small's. That was just a cellar, in a way of speaking. A pretty big cellar. It had sawdust on the floor and you know, these red and white table cloths and candles. And then that was -- that was the hotbed of real jazz. That's where you had people down there who played more jazz than you ever heard in your life. People can talk all they want about who played jazz and who didn't.
Well, he had Elmer Snowd@n was there and Roy, and Rex Stewart.....

Even before that. I never heard of Elmer Snowd@n or Rex Stewart. They were people I -- Freddie Jenkins -- Freddie Douglas. Freddie Douglas, he was a great waw-waw, man. Joe Williams, the trombone player. A guy they called Jazz, he used to be a drummer. And all kinds of piano players you never even heard of. Oh, those piano players. You know, that's when a girl used to go from table to table, all around the floor, you know. These piano players would just sit there with a mirror over the piano, you know, looking in the mirror to see what the girls were doing with the money, you know. A cigarette hanging. Beautiful piano players, oh, jeez, I'm telling you.

you first realize that jazz music was more than just, you know, a thing to do for a living or just something you enjoyed doing, that there were people really taking it seriously and studying it, that it was an important American music? Because most performers I talk to, most musicians say that back in those days there were no critics, and you know, no-one really -- no-one really thought of it being of historical importance, the things that were going on.

Well, I'll tell you, I realized that when -- well, I got the whole impact of the thing even when I first picked up a clarinet, because I knew then that all these things were happening, you know. Because I -- I hadn't got ahold of trade magazines or anything like that at that time, but there was -- the first thing -- the Metronome Magazine. Now, the Metronome Magazine was a classical magazine in the beginning.
Yes. It went back to the 1800's.

Yeah. And so then they shifted over. Every now and then they'd have an article about who was playing then and all the -- you know, then I realized that it was -- then by the time I got to -- I remember distinctly, by the time I go to the National School on 116th Street, you know, I was about 18 years old by then I guess. 18 or 17 or 18. Then I remember the first -- I don't remember who wrote the article and I don't remember what publication it was in, but I remember

somebody came down on Fletcher Henderson's band, and it said something about the band didn't sound good, or they didn't care what they were playing or something along that order, you know. Then I realized, oh, somebody's paying attention, you know. And this was real early, early in my career, you know. But music -- so at first I did realize that it was just part of the whole music scene, you know, because I -- that old Victrola at home that I've got, that my father used to buy these records. He used to buy this big Victor Red Seal records with Alma Gluck and Madame Tettrazini and Schumann-Heinck and all these people. And along with listening to them, I'd listen to them, and then I'd go down and I'd put on the next record by Ted Lewis, and I'd put on a record by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, and I'd put on a record by Mamie Smith, and it was all music, you know.
And of course much later you were doing a lot of classical music with Kirby, right?
Yeah. Yeah.

So then -- I could talk for three days about this, you know, details. So anyway, they found out that

-- then they began breaking up the -- our outfit was being broken up, you know, for -- this was when the war was at its worst. They had this big Battle of the Bulge incident. Then the order came down that no-one in the Armed Forces could move unless you were on the way to someplace. Wherever you are, stop, because everything's going to be turned around. So that broke up our band. It broke up the regiment and everything.

So then I remember I said to myself I was going to keep my nose clean and I wasn't going to -- least of all I wasn't going to get hurt, and I wasn't thinking about getting killed in nobody's army. So then I said now what'll I do? So we used to have -- in Huachuca, we used to call it -- the old post was an old National Guard post, and that's the post where Geronimo was captured by Captain White, in 1875, I think it was. That sort of thing. So there was a movie house up there, and these people had been living there, just like a little city, you know. And the (Unintelligible) down below was brand new, and it was all these barracks, and that's where the 92nd and 93rd colored divisions got trained. One went to Italy and one went to the Pacific. So by the time we got there we were the only outfit there, the 372nd Infantry.

So anyway, while we were there they broke it up, so I said now I'm going to have to do something. So this particular day I just got up -- they were doing different things. They were coming around and giving you different duties and so on.

One time I was in charge of quarters. I had to wake the soldiers up at 4:00 o'clock in the morning, and you stay up all night then you sleep all day. I was going through tremendous strain. So I just casually started walking one morning. I walked, must have been two miles. I just walked these two miles, thinking. So I said, well, I know what I'll do now. So I went to the movies and I went in a little cafeteria there and got something to eat and sat around. Then I went back to camp. Then I realized that I was AWOL. I said, that's good, but I didn't leave the camp. I was AWOL on the camp. So I kept that up for about a week. I kept it up for two weeks. I'd slip back in the barracks at night and go to sleep and get up early in the morning and leave again. So this one day the fellow came to me, one of the sergeants. He said, "The police are looking for you." You know, the military police. He said -- I said, "Well, that's simple. You just didn't see me. That's all." He said, "Well, they --," I said, "Well, don't worry about it. You just haven't seen me. Simple." So then finally, I kept it up, so then I realized that you know, you can't keep this up. You've got to do something. So I saw one of the Lieutenants, who was a recorder in the -- you know, they interview each soldier. You know, they was turning the whole thing around. So to cut it down, anyway, I said, "Well, do you think I should go to see these people who are looking for me?" He said, "Well, you know, what do you think? Do you

think you should?" I said, "Yes, I think I should now, because I would have to do something eventually. I can't keep this up." And I knew that if I'd run away, left the post and went home, you know, that would be worse. So I decided to go in front of the Board, you know. So I went to the barrack. I got all cleaned up, you know, and shaved. I guess I looked like an I don't know what, you know.

So I went in front of this Board. It was all white, and there was a Colonel, a Major and a Captain. Oh, they were heavy. Soldiers from Texas. Oh, my goodness. You're talking about soldiers, they were three soldiers. I mean soldiers. They didn't care. They didn't care what, they were soldiers, and they were about to whip everybody and win this war. So anyway, they called my name, you know, and I soldiered in the room and saluted. "Corporal Russell Procope reporting, sir." And they looked up at me and kept on writing. You know, they always give you that psychological treatment, you know. I'm way ahead of them, you know.

So then one looked up, so the Colonel says, "Where have you been? We've been looking for you for a week." I said, "Looking for me?" I said, "I've been right here. Nobody said anything to me." You know. So he had a few more, you know, wanted to know. He said, "Where did you get those stripes?" I said, "Well, I was in a band and I got the stripes in the band and the band's broken up now. There's no more
band." You know? He looked at me.

So the next fellow, I never will forget him. He had a crew cut, big husky fellow, looked like a football player. He was the Major. He said, "Let me talk to him." He said, "Now, you said in this -- they had this interview with you some time ago and you put down what was wrong with you." There wasn't nothing wrong with me. I said I have headaches all the time and my feet bother me. He says, "You have headaches?" I said yes. "And your feet bother you?" I said yes. You know what he said? He said, "They weren't bothering you when you was with John Kirby, were they?"
(Laughter)

I said, "Oh." So then that took some of the pressure off. Then he talked to me. He was probably a fan, and he -- so that blew over. So when I came out, they have, like I told you, they call them a recorder. He takes down what goes on during the -- so I said to this fellow, he was a young fellow, a young colored fellow, you know, a college man, you know. He was a Lieutenant. So I came out and they were doing everything with soldiers. They were throwing them on a train, shipping them overseas. I didn't know what was going to happen to me then. So I figured I'd give myself up, and I'd lost.
Well, anyway, I said to the recorder, I said, "What do you think they're going to do with me?" He says, "Well, I'll

tell you what I think. I think the worst that could happen to you was this Major will ship you down to Texas at his camp, so we could have you down there to play for him, or something like that." So I said, well, that wouldn't be so bad, you know.

But as it turned out I went back to my regiment and the Colonel -- the Colonel had what everyone called untouchables. I was one of the Colonel's untouchables. When you came to get soldiers, he had a file on this side that was the untouchables, and there was a file on that side which was the touchables. I was one of the untouchables. So the Colonel transferred me to the medics. I became a member of the Medical Corps, which I loved. It was beautiful. I loved that sort of thing, you know. I found I loved it, you know. You've got to administer to the -- you know, like -- and I took first aid training. You know, you had classes every morning. You learned to draw a skeleton and point out the parts. You know, a real medical setup. And we had doctors. Doctors were Captains and Majors and Colonels. To teach the classes every morning. It was beautiful, that phase of it. Then we went on bivouac up in the mountains. We slept in tents. It was wintertime. I backed out of the tent one morning into 10 feet of snow. But at that stage it was fine. I loved it.
In the meantime I got a letter from my brother who was overseas, in General Patton's Army, and he said to me, "Whatever you can do to keep from coming overseas, you do it."

"Even if it means going to jail." He said, "You go to jail. Don't come over here." Because my brother went all the way across the channel, clean on to Berlin with General Patton, and he saw the worst of it. He came back from the war with six battle stars. Yes, sir.

So, getting back, Colonel Gardine -- now, imagine, to show you how tight our outfit were, we were in a clearing. You know, we'd get up in the morning and build a fire and sit around the fire, in the winter, cold you know. So I saw these bushes, and lo and behold here comes the Colonel, Colonel Gardine. You know, he made out like it was an official visit. So everybody jumped up and stood at attention. He said, "As you were. At ease." He says, "Where's --," What was the Captain's name? "Where's Captain Barry --," I think it was. "Where's Captain Barry?" Said, "I don't know, sir, he was around here a little while ago. But I think he'll be back. I think he just went down to the first aid tent or something like that. So he looked at me and he said, "Come here. You'll do." I said, "He come to get the Colonel, and I'll do?" Anyway, I went with him. So the Colonel said to me, he says, "Have you heard from the old post?" I said, "No." He said, "Well, you will." He said, "I'm sending you up to the old post. You don't have to go overseas." And he says, "Anybody you want to take with you, just let me know and you can take them with you." How's that for a two-striper?
(Captain)
That's fantastic.

So he said, 'Well, you'll hear from them.' Then he left. So I went -- I was so happy, I told some of the fellows sitting around, I said, 'The Colonel's going to transfer me up to the old post, with the band.' I said, 'Any of you fellows want to go with me? You can if you want to, you know.' And I remember one fellow spoke up and said, 'No, we want to stick together.' I said, 'Okay, forget it.' And I turned my back and I left. And a couple of days later, here comes a fellow in a station wagon, took me and all my gear and everything. There was one other fellow the Colonel sent with me. He was a fellow who was a drummer in the band, you know, so it wouldn't look like -- he sent the two of us. I think this other fellow was a Sergeant or something. He said the tour was up to the old post.

Now, the old post, like I told you before, you know, was an old -- old Army, regular Army installation, which went way back to the Indian fighting. They met some of the wagons. The still kept up the tradition of horses and wagons and the fellows used to get the horses out and hitch them up on Sunday morning, and ride around, when they didn't have anything else to do, you know. Huachuca since became a missile base. That's what it is now, a missile base. So it came full circle from cavalry, horses, to missile base. Yeah.
So then that's where I spent the rest of the war. And we had -- oh, it was a beautiful barrack, and that barrack had been there, the old fashioned, I supposed a lot of Indian

fighters slept in it at one time. A real old wreck, about 1870, but of course you know the Army, they don't have anything to do but to find something to do. So they kept it in good condition all those years and everything.

Like in order to go to the shower, take a shower, you had to walk outside the building, you know, in the winter-time, and it's funny how healthy you are when you're in the Army. You don't realize it. In the Army you could sleep in a barrack with 40 soldiers in just one barrack, and you don't hear anybody say (Coughing). You don't hear anybody blowing their nose or nothing. You just hear this even breathing. And that's one good thing about the Army, they'll certainly get you in good condition, they certainly will. Physically you're perfect, as perfect as a man could be. A man has never been in as good condition as he was when he was in the Army, believe me.
Uh-huh.
So I spent the rest of my time in the old post where I was sent by Colonel Gardine, and my duties were we had one rehearsal a week, and every Saturday we had a parade, inspection parade.
Did you get any opportunity to play anything else?
Yes. Now, on the side, all through my Army career, we had different little dance bands, trios,
quartets, whatever we could get together to play jazz, dance music.
Any other musicians you were with whom we might know of?
Well, no, not in the -- most of the well known musicians who were drafted into the armed services were sent to Great Lakes.
Oh.
The Navy, which I abhored. I was so glad they didn't send me. I thought about all that, and I said now if they send me to Great Lakes and those Navy boys, I don't know what I'd have done, you know.
Was it just the uniform you didn't like, or --

That's right. I couldn't see myself walking with a little round white hat on and a cape hanging on my back, and this ribbon in front. To me that was a -- and I don't know, and it's the wrong image, because a sailor is always supposed to be the toughest human being ever invented, you know, down through history. Yeah.

So anyway, we did have little bands, like for instance when we were in Kentucky we -- of course in that area they had USO, you know, and the churches, and the ordinary people in town, like Evansville, Indiana was a short way from Breckenridge, and they'd hire us to play club date dances, just

like we were in civilian life. And for the USO shows we were paid $5.00, $5.00 a job, and we loved it because it was, you know, we could do what we wanted to do. We'd get away from it, you know. And I remember we had so much work that way, we used to work four or five nights a week. We were killing ourselves, and we'd get back. See, we were allowed to do this by the Colonel. And we'd just call up the office and say we need a truck, we're going to go to so-and-so, Henderson, Kentucky, or you know, whatever the town is. We're going 50 miles, 20 miles. And we'd go to the pool and get the truck and the driver and get in the truck and be driven to the job and he'd wait for us and drive us back to camp.
You had a very good deal there.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
So you were in there about two years.
Exactly.
So you came out in late '45.
Yeah, October, '45.
And then a couple of months later you were back in the Kirby band. What did you do when you first came out?

Well, I puttered around, you know. I was so glad to get out of the Army. I was free as a bird. I could flap my wings, you know. And it's quite an adjustment. And I think coming out of the Army was more of an adjustment than it was going in the Army, because you want to do so much.

You want to do and you want to regain what you lost in those two years, you know. And like that was two of the best years of my life, that sort of thing, you know. I wanted a car. I wanted to make a whole lot of money, you know. I wanted clothes. You know, everything. Everything. It was just a -- just a big change.

So anyway, I started just free lancing around, you know, getting jobs. I remember about the third or fourth day I was out of the Army, Charlie Holmes, you know, he came up to my house and he had a gig for me, which was, oh, beautiful, you know. I worked at Small's Paradise.
Charlie Holmes from Louis Russell's?
Yes, yes. So he was working in this band at Small's Paradise, and they needed a saxophone player, so he came and got me.
And then you went back with Kirby.

Yes, some time later. Let's see, this was -- this is in October. I think I went back with Kirby about October, November. Maybe in December. Because there was a little period in there where I was a -- where I was just having a good time, in a way of speaking, you know, renewing acquaintances or whatnot. I remember one night I came home from one of these jobs and my wife had gone to bed and she woke up, you know. We were having like a snack, you know, a midnight snack or something, and she said to me, she said,

"Don't you think you should bring some of that money home?" Because I've got into this thing I don't have to worry. You know, the Army sends an allotment home and you just eat and sleep, you know? Which was poor payment for what you were going through, I thought. And after they took out the allotment what I received out of it, out of my pay was $20.00 a month. See? But --
And no tips.

No tips. But you see, of course again I say I -- getting back to the Army -- I had it good. You know, I count my blessings. I realize that I had it damned good, because like Christmas and my birthday I'd get a tremendous amount of everything sent to me, and I'd tell everybody, don't send me no flowers. Don't send me no cakes. Because Uncle Sam's giving me all that. You just send me some money. And that's what I'd get, you know. My mother would send me money. My sister would send me money. You know, from everyplace I had it. That was good, yeah.
So it was at the Copacabana where I joined Kirby.
Where you rejoined him.
When I rejoined him, yes. And we followed Nat Cole and --
What shape did you find the Kirby band in when you came out? Who was with it? Had he kept it going in the two years?

He kept it going, but it wasn't -- it wasn't -- it wasn't. He had a -- he had Bill Beason on drums, Hank Jones on piano. I mean these are good musicians, but they weren't getting the, you know, original sound or the original --
Was Buster still there?
Yes. Yes. And he had a trumpet player who has since died. His name was Freddy Webster.
Oh, yeah.
Freddy Webster, which was a very good -- he was a very good trumpet player, but he went the way those young be-boppers were going then, you know.
What about a pianist?
Hank Jones was the pianist.
Oh, that's right, you mentioned Hank Jones.
Yes. Yes.
Yes. Now, be-bop wasn't really -- I guess it was just, '45 it was just coming in.
Just coming in.
Yeah.
Because Charlie --
Was that the first time you heard that?
The first time I heard it, I would say,

I was in the Army, and I visited 52nd Street, you know, one of my nights, you know, out. And Ben Webster was playing at one of the clubs. I don't remember which one it was. On 52nd Street. And I was around the corner in a bar, a bar where everybody, all the musicians, used to congregate, you know, drinking and conversation and what not. And Ben Webster came in and he said to me, "Come go with me, I want you to hear this saxophone player." "He's playing right now around the corner," and he took me around the corner and it was Charlie Parker. And that was my first thing, as I remember, brush with be-bop.
So you heard the master from the beginning.
That's right. That's right. That's right.
And what kind of effect did that have on you?

Well, I'll tell you. I sat there and I listened to him. Of course at that time I'd been playing about 15 years, so I could get an overall picture of what he was doing. You know, you could trace it. And I said, "He's a very good saxophone player. He's a very good saxophone player." And comparing him with, oh, the other saxophone players down through the years he was a very good saxophone player. He knew what he was doing and he was really very, very, very
good and he was very impressive. Yeah. And I think he was one of the great, one of the masters of the saxophone. I never heard anyone master saxophone like he did.
Technically.
Technically. Technically, like a typewriter. Yeah.
But the music was quite different. Because a lot of musicians didn't like it at first.

Well, no, and I'll tell you, I heard some music before that which, to use the expression that they use, way out. They use the expression way out, meaning if it's way out you don't know anything about it, you don't understand it, you don't like it or whatever, you say it's way out. But anyway, I always, from my training in music ever since I was very young, music is music. Of course people say but if you don't understand it it's like French. I could listen to you talk French all day. I don't know what the hell you're talking about. But if I go and study some French, then I'll understand you, right? Okay. So then I began buying these records and sitting and listening to them. And after awhile I began to understand it. I got the message, in other words.
So that was how it came about. And I'll go on record as saying that Charlie Parker influenced all the musicians, the piano players, the bass players, the trumpet players, all

of them. Charlie Parker influenced everyone who ever played jazz, and maybe some people who didn't play jazz. Charlie Parker was a great influence in music, let's put it that way. Absolutely. And all the rest of them came after him. And there's a tremendous, tremendous amount of people still studying Charlie Parker to this day.
Yeah.
And I believe he died young because it was supposed to happen that way. Goodness knows what he would have played if he had lived.
Right.
And I'm saying that from the standpoint of another musician, another saxophone player. And right now, today, I have eight-tracks of Charlie Parker.
Yeah?
I play them in the car.
Oh.
And I just sit there still, listen to him and marvel.
Now, the whole be-bop scene, it was -- when you went into the service, I guess 52nd Street was still going full guns.
Oh, yes. Oh, yes.
Swing music.
Yes.
And in the be-bop scene, drugs became more predominant.
Right.
Than they had before.
Right.
It was alcohol before.
Right. Right.
And reefer. And why do you suppose that all of a sudden it was -- so many of the be-boppers were strung out on drugs and they died young because of it?

Well, I don't know. I wouldn't attempt to say why. I don't know. I suppose it was, for one thing, I would say that, well, just in my judgment, you know, I don't know, but just a stab at it and try to answer that question, maybe it was the stress of the times.
Uh-huh.

What with the war and the activity which it generated and a sort of a loose freedom that the people had in general. And naturally these fellows, coming up very young, they -- and not having any background to fall back on, and they weren't -- they hadn't formed any habits, I suppose they just reached out and took whatever was available.

Yeah.

Yeah. He was born around Christmas time and I was born in August. There was that difference in age. But he died a young man in California. He had diabetes. Yeah. Yeah. And he was drinking when he wasn't supposed to be drinking. said, "Has he been drinking?" I said yes. He always did drink. So she said he wasn't supposed to. Now, she should have told me that before. I didn't know that. So, lo and behold, he -- I never knew what he died from, but the way he died, I think he had a heart attack.
Uh-huh.
Seems as though he just gave one gasp and died, which sounds like a heart attack. Yeah.

Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. I couldn't take that, you know. And I couldn't -- in other words, doing what he was doing at that time wasn't furthering myself, wasn't in my groove, let's say, because there wasn't too much happening. And after the Copacabana closed, then I don't remember exactly, but sort of knocked around and knocked around, and then at one phase I couldn't find him for two weeks. I didn't even know where he was. He wasn't home. You know. So lo and behold, came this call from Duke Ellington. So by this time he was back, he appeared on the scene, and he offered me everything not to go with Duke. But I realized that he wasn't going anywhere at that time, and so I told him, I said, "Well, I just spent two years in the Army and I'm trying to get
