I was going to say you didn't think you were going to stay there forever.
No. No. So anyway, I joined Duke Ellington.
What was that like? Was it what you had expected it would be like?

Well, in a way yes, and in a way, no. You see, when you see something from afar you get one image, and when you know it from within it's another image, which holds for Duke Ellington's band. There were a lot of things that were happening in the band that the general public, you know, when they go see Duke Ellington on the stage, they're all dressed up in the white suits and the shiney instruments and whatnot, you know, but when I got into the band, you know, I think I got on the bus, I think I rode the bus for two or three weeks before I even said anything. Just observing and absorbing and listening to the people in the band, their conversation, you know. The past incidents, what happened and whatnot, you know, just getting the whole story together of the band. Yeah.
Well, you know the old story about joining Duke for one night and staying 28 years. Well, that's a fact, because
he called me to play this important Saturday afternoon broadcast in Worcester, Massachusetts. So I went there. I went up to Massachusetts that afternoon and played the broadcast with him, and --
Replacing someone?
Replacing Otto Hardwicke.
Uh-huh.

And I played the broadcast, and he said, 'Well, since you're here we're playing a dance tonight in Providence, Rhode Island. Why don't you come and play with us?' So I said, 'Okay, since I'm up here in New England.' You know. I mean I wasn't too anxious to join Duke, you know, as such, you know.
Uh-huh.

Right then. Right then at that moment, because it meant leaving home again, which I had just got out of the Army and I'd been away from home a little bit. But incidentally, the longest I was away from home when I was in the Army was eight months. That's the longest period I was away from home.

So when I joined Duke, you know, it was sort of I had to make a decision. I wanted to, you know, get back on my feet, you know, and have some money in my pocket and whatnot. So I decided, well, I said to my -- if he offered me the -- he hadn't offered me the job. I was just filling in for

someone else, Otto Hardwick. So one word led to another and so he was playing New England and he was coming back to New York. So we talked from day to day. So I decided that, well, I'd just finish this little trip, then I'd be back home, you know. Then I discovered he was going to play the Paramount (Laughs) Theater for six weeks. / So one day we were up in Hartford. There was a theater all the bands used to play on Sunday. I think it was the Star Theater, the Star Theater. All the bands, you know, they'd have a big show on Sunday, just one day. They'd have singers, you know, acts. So he called me. Then he really talked to me then. He said, 'I'll tell you what. I don't know whether this guy, Hardwick, I don't know where he is, and --,' I think he called him a nut or something else. He said, 'I don't know what this nut's going to do.' So he said, 'Why don't you stay? Why don't you stay with us.' You know, 'I think you'd like it.' 'Yeah, well, how much would you want?' You know, that sort of thing. And I told him. And he agreed, okay, you know. So I was hired. And this was after I'd been in the band about 10 days. So I remember after about five days or so, I said, you know, by that time I was talking. I had got the lay of the land, and I was sitting about the fourth seat back, Duke sat up in the front seat, and I said, 'Hey, Duke.' And he said, 'Huh?' And I said, 'Who's supposed to pay me?' I said it loud, you know, so everybody could hear what I'm saying. And he said, 'You mean you haven't

had any money since you've been here?" I said no. And all the fellows looked at me, you know, wondering how am I getting along. They didn't know that I'd sent home to my wife for some money in the meantime. So when I sent it -- when I sent home for the money, Johnny Hodges knew I'd -- you know, because I think he knew I'd gone to Western Union or something. So Johnny called me aside. He said, "Now, you didn't have to do that. You didn't have to send home for money." I said, "Well, I didn't know the ropes, you know." Then I found out this guy sitting up front with the glasses was the manager. Al Colley Sully, you know.
Uh-huh.
He's the guy you're supposed to ask for money. You know, I didn't know. I'm used to working for a man, if I'm working --
No-one told you.
No-one told me, right. You know, if you're working for Jim Jones you ask Jim Jones for the money. But this is big time. He had a manager.

Well, anyway, to make a story, that's the way it happened, and of course it went down and we played the six weeks at the Paramount Theater, which was real beautiful, real fine. And I remember between shows, they were getting ready to close the last week of the engagement, and I remember talking to Harry Carney, we were between shows, standing on

the sidewalk on 44th Street. I didn't even have any bags. You know, these guys, they've got their bags and they've been doing it for years.. So I said, "Well, what do you think kind of bags I should get, you know?" He said, "Well, most of the fellows have a big bag, what they call the big bag, and a small bag." That's what they called them. Oh. So I said, "Okay, I'll go buy a big bag and a small bag." So I bought a big bag and a small bag. The big bag was like a trunk, you know, and they kept that under the bus, and you carried your little bag with you, you know, with a shirt and your toothbrush and whatnot, so if you wanted to change your suit you'd go get your big bag. We had a valet, he had a valet. Duke Ellington had a famous valet named Jonesy.
Yes.

Jonesy was Duke's man. Jonesy was a young fellow who Duke got from the Cotton Club. He was a bus boy up at the Cotton Club, and he got very friendly with Duke and Duke's band when they were up at the Cotton Club, and when Duke left the Cotton Club, he left and went along with Duke as, you know, a valet, a band boy or whatever. So Jonesy was along, you know, and whatever you wanted, just tell Jonesy. You'd say, "Jonesy, get my big bag." That's all you had to say and Jonesy would get your big bag and put it in the hotel lobby. You'd get a bellboy to take your big bag up to the room. Everything was beautiful. You know, you didn't have
to -- and they'd even carry your instruments for you.
That was a big band. Jonesy must have been very busy.
He was. He was.
Whatever happened to Jonesy?

Jonesy? He -- I think he was an asthmatic, because I remember one night we were on this pullman train, we were on this pullman, and I came -- I woke up in the middle of the night and I climbed down out of the berth and I went in the smoker, and there was Jonesy, sitting there, gasping, and I remember taking him and opening the -- you know, those trains had dutch doors, you opened the -- and sticking his head out the window so he could get this air, you know. He sort of had an attack, you know. So it got worse and worse, you know, and he finally died from that. I don't remember exactly when he died, but he did.
That was such a big band. Was there much unity in the band or were there little cliques and saxophone players stick together and trumpet players stick together?

Well, there's a sort of a little joke about that, because, as I say, people on the outside didn't know what went on on the inside of the band. So the musicians who weren't in the band, you know, all of the musicians about town, they'd say to me, 'Well, how are you getting along?'

Then they'd say, "They tell me that they have cliques in the band." So I'd say, "Cliques? Well, if they have cliques in the band I must belong to all of them, because I don't know anything about it." Which I didn't. But you must realize that I've known these fellows.
Yeah.
And they knew me, see? And this period when I told you, I didn't -- I had practically nothing at all to say when I was riding the bus, because I was sort of learning the fellows.
Yeah.
Because you never really know a man till you work with him or live with him. That's how you get to know a man. So that's what it was.
What had happened to Toby?

Well, he just -- he was gone. But Toby -- because Toby was my friend, too, because he was one of the first musicians I met when I first started playing, and he told me. So every time I'd see him, he'd sort of give me advice about the band, you know. He'd say, "Don't let them do this to you, because they'll do this to you.
Well, he should know.
He should know. And, "Don't let Duke do this to you. Watch him." I remember Johnny Hodges telling me, you know, about the first week in the band. He said,

"Listen, if you go to tell Duke anything, be sure you know what you want to say when you go to him, and say it." You know. Then I found out that was the right thing to do, and Toby, he too would tell me, like I said, what to do and what not to do. And Toby, I remember Toby made some records when he left the band. I remember he recorded -- oh, what is the name of that, from, "Black, Brown and --," "Come Sunday."
Uh-huh.
I remember he recorded "Come Sunday," and you know, he had record dates. Then he sort of went back to Washington and drifted out of the business.
He did?
Yeah.

You know, it's been said that very Duke very often took credit, too much credit, that not enough credit was given to individual members of the band who had a hand in, you know, creating compositions and sounds. Any validity to that?

That's true, and what -- yeah, I can move over here. That's true, because you see, Duke Ellington was a man -- Duke Ellington was what we used to call in the old days a hustler. Duke liked to say he was raised in a pool room, which he wasn't actually, but that gave you an inkling as to his background and what he knew. In other words, he was a man of the world, which he was, who could cope with any
situation, which he could, and who could cope with any person or any type of person, which he could.

Now, when Duke was coming up, when he started, Irving Mills was his mentor, I guess you'd say, and every bar of music Duke Ellington wrote, Irving Mills' name was on it. Irving -- and Duke Ellington used to write all this music and he used to write a tremendous amount of blues and things, you know, or bluesy type things, which contributed to his reputation. I mean moreso than just playing the average popular songs. So Duke got that idea. So I think consciously or subsonsciously or whatever, he was getting back at Irving Mills.
I see. He was making up for his lost --

That's right. That's right. And I firmly -- and I knew that when I was in the band. If you wrote something, and he wouldn't say, but he'd get an idea from it, and people used to say -- and sometimes it would be more subterfuge than anything else -- they'd -- a lot of people used to say that Duke Ellington was the biggest thief in the business. And that could be said about a lot of other people in the business, without mentioning any names. Of course you know that.
Oh, sure.
So that's the reason I think there's a lot of validity, like you say, in that statement.
What about Billy Strayhorn?
Billy Strayhorn -- I think it was 1939 when Billy Strayhorn joined Duke, right?
Yeah.

Yeah. Now, Duke Ellington hired Billy Strayhorn to write lyrics. In other words they'd have a team. Duke would write the music and Billy Strayhorn would write the lyrics. Billy Strayhorn was one of the most brilliant men I've ever known. Billy Strayhorn would have been successful, tremendously successful in any line of endeavor he chose to follow. He would have been a brilliant doctor. He would have been a brilliant lawyer. He would have been just anything. A smart man. Now, he was a piano player, a brilliant piano player, and so I said, 'Well, now, Billy, how is it you started arranging this music?' He said, 'Well, I'll tell you.' Duke didn't actually teach him, but he left these scores around and he -- so Billy could -- he'd give them to him, you know, because Billy was a brilliant pianist. And that's the way Billy learned to arrange. Like that. (Snaps fingers)
(Snaps fingers)
And Billy had the reputation of being one of the best arrangers ever, and that includes everybody. Believe me. So in that case, Duke was doubly blessed.
Now, Billy Strayhorn was -- was in demand by everybody in the world. I mean, you know, Hollywood people. But Billy was satisfied to stay with Duke all those years. I

suppose for the same reason I stayed with Duke and a lot of other people stayed with Duke, because you had a tremendous amount of freedom to do what you want and all that, and Billy made a whole lot of money from his, you know, songs and arrangements, and that's part of Billy Strayhorn's story.

But you always -- I mean if it's an Ellington-Strayhorn tune, it's always mentioned as an Ellington tune. You know, a lot of -- we who are in the business, we know about Billy Strayhorn, and some other people knew of course. Most people don't really think of Strayhorn.
No, no! That's right.
He was really in the shadow of Duke. It must have been frustrating.
Oh, yes. I don't think it was frustrating for him. He was satisfied --
Yeah.
-- with the life he was living. And he lived a good life. Because he was on the payroll.
Uh-huh.
And Duke must have paid him -- he probably -- I don't know, but he must have, you know, had a very good contract with Duke, judging from the way he lived and, you know, everything.
Is that right.
Yeah. And sometimes we wouldn't see
Billy for months. He just wasn't doing anything. He was just in New York while we were on the road, living, just living.
Right.

Then all of a sudden Duke would have this tremendous amount of work for him, writing music, and he'd sit there days, weeks, writing these suites and numbers, and he was a great arranger of vocals, vocal songs.
Did he spend much time in Paris, because he was a very close friend of Aaron Bridges, wasn't he?
Yeah. Well, they were friends before, in New York.
Oh.
Yeah. Then he went to -- yeah, Aaron was playing at the Living Room in Paris.
Yes.
Yeah. And just to show you what kind of a guy Billy was, we went to Paris, and Duke called Billy out on the stage and he addressed the audience in French. He spoke to the audience in French.
Yeah?
Yeah. Yeah, he was some kind of man. I remember we were walking down the street in Paris one day, and every sign I saw, I'd just ask Billy, "What does that

mean? What does that say?" And he'd tell me. Yeah. Yeah. Very, very unassuming person. You wouldn't think he -- you know, I wouldn't say insignificant, but very unassuming person. He wore those thick rimmed glasses.
Right.
He looked like a little professor or something. Yeah.
So Duke knew full well what he had in him.
He certainly did. He certainly knew what he had.
So that must have been quite a loss when he died.
Yeah. Billy could get anything he wanted, including a $5,000.00 piano.
Yeah.
That's right. Billy used to say, 'You see, that's my car over there. I don't want a car. That's my car over there,' and he'd point to his piano.
Oh. What about Ruth? Was she involved at all?

Well, that's another story. I don't care to get involved in that, because it won't prove anything. What I have to say about all these things -- I don't think -- to my mind that's an invasion of privacy. I don't mind, you
know, talking, but I've seen other people interviewed, writing books and things, but that's one phase of the Duke Ellington band or company or what have you that I don't care to discuss or get into.

I don't know what I'm talking about. I was just curious about Ruth's role in the whole thing. I mean I don't -- I know Ruth, and I know that she seems to keep up with what's happening as far as the tunes are concerned, but I didn't know whether she had any function at all with the band. Got involved at all, or just stayed in the background. So when I asked you -- obviously there's something there you don't want to tell me, but I didn't know. I wasn't fishing for something.
No, you're saying something there --
Very often there is a woman who makes a decision. I wanted to ask you about Mrs. Henderson. Remember, when you were talking about Mrs. Henderson.
Yeah.

I was listening last night to an interview I have with Lester Young, where Lester said when he came to the Henderson band, Mrs. Henderson took him downstairs and played him Coleman Hawkins, and she was the one, not Fletcher, she was the one who played him the Coleman Hawkins records and was trying to get him to sound like Coleman Hawkins. You know, so there was a woman who obviously had
more influence than one would think.
Yes, but the fact of the matter is Mrs. Henderson was a musician.
Right, exactly. Right. A big difference.
Of course.

But she wasn't the leader of the Henderson band, though. I just found that interesting that, you know, Fletcher apparently -- I mean Lester, from the tone of his voice, I gathered didn't appreciate that. He felt that she was interfering, you know, that it wasn't her business.
In other words he didn't believe in women's lib.
(Laughter)

Well, you know, maybe if she'd done something else. But you know, it's something to take a Lester Young and tell him to sound like Coleman Hawkins. I'm sure you're off to a wrong start there immediately.
Well, since you brought that point up, Lester Young at that period in his life wasn't Lester Young. You understand what I mean.
Right. Right.
You understand. He hadn't established himself for the great tenor saxophone player that he later became.
Right.
And he certainly was a great tenor player. But at that stage of the game he wasn't. So you could see that it makes sense.

Oh, sure. Although he obviously was not playing in the Coleman Hawkins style. He obviously had his own thing going even then. Something different from Coleman Hawkins. If she was trying to get him -- I guess it was his tone. He probably didn't have the rich tone of Coleman Hawkins, right? But anyway, getting back to Duke's band, you stayed with it so long. Was it because of security or was it because you enjoyed it? Doesn't one get tired of playing the same arrangements so many times?

Duke Ellington kept his band and his music up to date. Now, like I was telling some people last night, Duke, he listened to a -- for instance, we have certain tunes which are popular, like take, "Solitude," for instance. During the time I was in the band Duke must have made 15 different arrangements on, "Solitude," on, "Sophisticated Lady," "Mood Indigo," those type of things which were popular and which he had many, many requests for.
He kept updating them.
He'd bring them up to date. Kept updating them all the time. So naturally they didn't become stagnant to the band. And Duke's whole repertoire changed and

changed and changed. And if you -- so for instance, after I was in the band 10 years, I could look back on -- and also listen to the recordings, what we played then. And after I was in the band 15 years I could look back and see, and I'd say, "Oh, did I do that? Oh, that's terrible. Did I play that? Oh." You know, right up to the last. So that didn't -- it wasn't that way.
Now, Rex Stewart told me once that Duke always encouraged his men to compose. Did he actually encourage you? Did he go out of his way to encourage you to compose, or was he just open to it?

Well, I wouldn't say that he encouraged you, but if you did have a -- you know, if you were inclined that way he wouldn't, you know, stop you. And he'd let you make your arrangement and he'd have the band play it, and if he thought it worthy to play, you know, he'd do it. If he didn't think it was worthy he wouldn't have too much to say, but he just wouldn't use it.
So I guess that is a form of encouragement, the fact that it was possible.
Oh, yes, of course. Oh, in that sense yes, yes. Yes, yes. Uh-huh.
But -- I had a question.
I must have played, 'Mood Indigo,'

5,000 times while I was in the band. And really, every time I played it it was a new experience, because every time you thought you'd put a little twist there, a different gliss there or something, because like everything we played in Duke's band, what you did to what you were playing added to -- you know, you just didn't play note for note what you played every night, you know.
What did you think of Duke's various vocalists?

Oh, gee whiz, he had so many vocalists. I remember I asked Tony Watkins, who was Duke's last -- excuse me -- last vocalist, I said, "Tony, how many girl singers has Duke had since you've been the male vocalist?" He said nine. And to my mind Tony was only with the band a short time. You know, comparatively.
Right.
So he must have had I don't know how many girl vocalists.

Well, I always found a strange disparity there. I found that very few of his singers matched his musicians, you know, as far as real talent is concerned. I always thought that for the band that it was he had remarkably inferior singers.
Well, now, that's a thing I would say generally that you're right. But I suppose -- I don't know,

but I suppose Duke thought that all he wanted a vocalist to do was sing one or two songs or three or four songs a night. And they didn't have to be Ella Fitzgerald or Sarah Vaughan to sing these songs, because the people that were hearing songs, some of them for the first time, and they probably wouldn't hear them again till the next time they heard Duke's band. And the people who recorded with Duke, if you listen to records, you'll see that Duke recorded them very well. Plus the arrangements that were around these vocalists, you know, that added to it. And the vocalists sang of course, and maybe somebody like Ray Nance would come out and play eight bars and it all added to it. Then the complete thing was there, like a show. You know. It was show business, I think.
But he did some very innovative things in the early days, with Baby Cox, when he had her growling and smiling, you know.
Yeah.
And with Adelaide Hall.
Yeah.
And later Kay Davis.
Yeah. Yeah.
And then it was a big jump, it seems to me, from that -- and then Ivie Anderson, of course. But when he then went to Joya Sherrill and Tony Watkins, you know, it was kind of a letdown.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
It just -- it seemed a discrepancy there. I never really understood why that was. But I guess your information is probably right, that he didn't see the vocalist as that --
That's right.
Their function was a minor function.

The vocalist was just a part of what was going on, not to be a featured singer, not to be a star as such. If, after they came with the band, they became a star, that was something else. But he wasn't going around looking to hire any stars, you know. Like I don't doubt that an Ella Fitzgerald or a Sarah Vaughan or a Lena Horne, somebody like that, you know, after they were a big name, then he'd hire them to sing with the band, you know. Then everybody would say, 'Oh, wow, Lena Horne singing with Duke!' You know. But it wasn't that way.
Well, I think that's -- can you think of anything that we haven't covered? We've got Duke. After you left Duke you were ill. What was wrong with you then?
Oh, after I was --
In '71, yes.
Yeah.
I -- well, the way I say it --
It was while you were with Duke, right?

Yeah, while I was with Duke. I prefer to say I just ran out of gas. Put it that way. And my blood pressure, it was so high it's a wonder it didn't blow the top of my head off. And it took the doctors weeks to even get it down a little bit, because you know, during my time I drank a tremendous amount of whiskey. I did a tremendous amount of carousing. I did everything that a man could do without killing himself. I probably got to the point of killing myself without knowing it, which I really did. So -- and I walked up to -- of course I hadn't been sick a day in my life. And really, I worked with Duke Ellington -- the 28 years I worked with Duke Ellington, I don't think I missed a month's work in the 28 years. Duke Ellington's bus had an accident once, and I had my back strained a little bit. Of course I made a big hulabaloo out of it, a court case and all that sort of stuff, you know. And I got, you know, some money out of it, and I think I was out of the band then about a month. I was in the hospital and, you know, that sort of thing. I think that's the only thing that kept me out of the band.
Were there vacations for the band?
No. Duke? No, no vacations.
Nobody had a vacation.
Well, if you took one, you know.
You could take a vacation.
Yeah.
But it wasn't as if the whole band stopped.

The whole band, no. No, no, no. If Duke could work 365 days a year, he'd do it. Yes, you could, you know, tell him, 'I'm going to take two weeks off,' and he'd put somebody in your place or he'd get somebody in your place, you know.
So your blood pressure, and you stopped. But then you went back to the band.
Oh, yes. Yes. You see --
How long were you out?

Oh, I had a complete rest. I think it was about 4 months, 5 months, something like that. Then again, which was a third phase in my life that I had to readjust. I had two phases before that and this was the third. So -- and you don't know how a man -- and you can lay in the bed in the hospital and think. Oh, I'm telling you. You count all the bricks in the building. You count all the spokes in the bed. You count all the footsteps that you hear out in the hallway, and so on. But then I realized that I had to stop doing a lot of things I had been doing and start doing a lot of things, you know, vice-versa. So I

-- and then, as I say, it's a complete adjustment, because you don't know how you'll feel when you come out of the hospital and come back home. It's a new thing, believe me. You're scared to cross the street. You see the traffic coming. You know, you're just like a little child. That sort of thing. So anyway, I adjusted and I got back.
I remember Duke was playing -- what's the name of the place over in Central Park? The Wellmann --
The skating rink?
The skating rink.
The Wollman Memorial Rink.

Yeah. So he was playing there, so I went over there one day. I think I was just starting getting back, getting my horn, you know, getting my fingers to working, and I had been down to Pleasantville, New Jersey. You know, we have a place down there, you know, sort of a summer home, I guess you'd call it, and I'd been spending time down there. And I remember I went to Atlantic City and brought some reeds, when I decided to start blowing again. So I went by this Memorial, and Duke was playing there. He had an afternoon concert and a night concert. So I went to hear the band and I went backstage after the afternoon performance, and I had my horn with me, so Duke said, 'Well, come on, play this next show.' I said, 'Oh, no. No, no. I'm not ready.'
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
